## Introduction

You're choosing a city to start your career in. A cost-of-living website
scores 150 cities around the world on six things. Six scores per city is
too many to compare at once: PCA turns them into a few, and draws the
cities on a map of two numbers. By the end, you'll pick your city and
decide whether the map helped.

| Column | Meaning | Better when |
|---|---|---|
| `purchasing` | what a local salary buys (purchasing power) | higher |
| `health` | quality of health care | higher |
| `cost` | prices of everyday goods (New York = 100) | lower |
| `pollution` | air and water pollution | lower |
| `safety` | how safe residents feel | higher |
| `climate` | how pleasant the weather is | higher |

The data have two more scores, `property` (home prices ÷ incomes) and
`commute` (time spent commuting). We leave them out until Part 3.

**Estimated time: 20 minutes.** The goal for today is the first look at
the data and **Parts 1–3**. If you finish them, keep going with the
**Bonus** section at the end. If you don't reach the Bonus, that's
completely fine.

Each task ends with a question in *italics*. Write a sentence or two for each.

```{r load}
cities <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mgelman/data/master/livable_cities.csv")

# Short column names
cities <- cities %>%
  rename(city = City, country = Country, quality = `Quality of Life Index`,
         purchasing = `Purchasing Power Index`, safety = `Safety Index`,
         health = `Health Care Index`, cost = `Cost of Living Index`,
         property = `Property Price to Income Ratio`,
         commute = `Traffic Commute Time Index`, pollution = `Pollution Index`,
         climate = `Climate Index`)

# The six scores PCA gets to see
X <- cities %>% select(purchasing, health, cost, pollution, safety, climate)
```

### A first look at the data (2 minutes)

```{r look}
round(cor(X), 2)      # correlation of every pair of columns
```

*Find the two most strongly correlated columns. Do these six columns go
together as much as the colleges' did on the slides (every pair between
0.39 and 0.67), or less?*

## Part 1: The Components (7 minutes)

Remove the `#`s. The middle lines flip the signs (see "Signs are
arbitrary" on the slides) so that a high PC1 means high purchasing power
and a high PC2 means safe.

```{r task1}
# pca <- prcomp(X, scale = TRUE)
#
# s1 <- sign(pca$rotation["purchasing", 1])     # +1 or -1
# s2 <- sign(pca$rotation["safety", 2])
# pca$rotation[, 1] <- s1 * pca$rotation[, 1];  pca$x[, 1] <- s1 * pca$x[, 1]
# pca$rotation[, 2] <- s2 * pca$rotation[, 2];  pca$x[, 2] <- s2 * pca$x[, 2]
#
# summary(pca)$importance[2:3, ]      # proportion of variance explained, and cumulative
# round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2)       # loadings on PC1 and PC2
```

*How much of the variation does PC1 keep, and PC1 and PC2 together? How
many components do you need to keep 80%?*

*Which columns have the biggest PC1 loadings, and with which signs? So what
kind of city has a high PC1 score?*

*PC2 is a trade-off, like "the mix" on the slides. Which two columns does it
use? What does a city gain, and what does it give up, as PC2 goes up?*

*Using your answers to Part 1, describe the cities in each corner of the

on PC2? Which corner would you want to live in, given what you care about?*

---

## Part 3: Pick Your City (4 minutes)

Pick a city from your corner of the map: a labeled one, or one from the
tables above. Fill in its name, and remove the `#`s. The output shows
all eight of its scores, including `property` and `commute`, which PCA
didn't see, next to the median city.

```{r task3}
# my_city <- "___"
#
# cities %>% filter(city == my_city) %>% select(city, purchasing:climate, PC1, PC2)
# cities %>% summarise(across(purchasing:climate, median))     # the median city
```

*Which city did you pick, and why? Do its original scores hold any
surprises the map hid? Do `property` and `commute` change your mind? Did
the two components help you choose, or would you rather have compared the
six scores directly?*
